title: Incident orchestration patterns and practice lab
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Overview

Purpose: This page defines repeatable incident orchestration patterns, a compact runbook template, and a companion practice lab (game-day) curriculum. It is aimed at on-call responders, SREs, and engineering managers who run drills and maintain responder muscle memory for production degradations.

Scope: patterns for detection -> triage -> containment -> remediation -> recovery -> post-incident learning. Includes standard role definitions, SLO-triggered escalation timings, status page and customer messaging templates, plus a postmortem checklist and retro template.

Owner: Platform Reliability (eng-sre)
Maintainers: oncall rotation leads, runbook working group

Quick links:
- Runbook template (below)
- Sample status-page messages and customer email templates (section: Communications)
- Game-day schedule and rubric (section: Practice lab)

1) Incident orchestration patterns

1.1 Roles and responsibilities- Incident Commander (IC): owns decision making, customer comms cadence, and declaring incident severity.
- Bridge Engineer: triage the signal in the live bridge and own debugging pipeline.
- Service Owner: subject matter expert for the impacted service; coordinates fixes and releases.
- Customer Liaison: product/support rep for outbound customer messages.
- Runbook Author: keeps the runbook accurate and performs runbook post-exercise updates.

1.2 Severity and escalation ladder (SLO-aligned)
| Severity | Effect | SLO breach threshold | Primary response SLA | Escalation point |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Sev-1 | Complete outage or sustained >90% error rate | Error budget depleted within 30m | IC on-call within 5m, full bridge within 15m | Pager to Director on 30m
| Sev-2 | Partial outage or significant feature degradation | Error budget burn >50% in 1h | Bridge and owner within 15m | Escalate to SRE lead after 1h
| Sev-3 | Intermittent failures, elevated latency | Degraded for >4h or user-facing regression per customer reports | Owner notified within 60m | Review during next day sync

Notes: timing targets are operational goals. Use judgment when customer impact is asymmetric (high-value customers affected).

1.3 Pattern: Fast containment, slow recovery
- Contain first: if safe, route traffic away, enable degraded mode, or scale pools.
- Quarantine problem components to prevent blast radius.
- Prioritize restoring accepted traffic over full feature parity.

1.4 Pattern: Canary -> Rollback -> Patch
1. Verify whether a recent rollout correlates with the incident.
2. If yes, trigger an immediate rollback of the canary wave.
3. If rollback is not possible, enable a safe fallback (previous model variant, reduced consistency) and continue debugging.

2) Runbook template (compact)

Title: [Service name] - Compact incident runbook
Scope: One-line summary of what the runbook covers
Signal sources: List of alerts, dashboards, customer reports, third-party monitoring
Initial checks (first 5 minutes):
1. Confirm alert validity (metrics vs alert flapping).
2. Identify scope: regions, customers, endpoints.
3. Grab recent deploy history: `git log --since=\"2 hours\" --oneline`
4. Open bridge and assign roles.

Containment steps (choose minimal-impact option first):
- Disable autoscaler or set manual min replicas (CLI example):
```
kubectl scale deployment service-api --replicas=10 -n prod
```
- Route traffic away (example, feature-flag rollback):
```
redwoodctl flags set --project=payments payments.v2=false
```

Recovery steps (iterative):
1. Attach profiler and collect a 60s flame sample.
2. Examine thread dumps and GC metrics.
3. If a config or env var is suspect, revert and test.
4. If a code rollback is needed: verify artifact hash, roll back, and monitor for 15 minutes.

Post-incident chores (short list):
- Owner: file postmortem within 72 hours.
- Runbook Author: update runbook within 7 days with the discovered mitigation.
- SRE Lead: schedule any required follow-up release or test.

3) Communication templates

Status page short-form (initial notice):
"We are investigating elevated errors impacting the [SERVICE NAME] in [REGION]. Customers may see request failures and increased latency. We will provide updates every 30 minutes. Impacted customers: [If known, list]."

Status page update (containment):
"We have implemented a mitigation to reduce customer impact (traffic reroute / scaled replicas). Error rates have declined by ~X%. We are continuing to monitor and will share a recovery ETA soon."

Customer email template (when impact affects billing-critical flows):
Subject: Incident affecting [SERVICE] in [REGION] — immediate update
Body: Hello [Customer Name],
We detected an issue affecting [SERVICE] starting at [time]. Our engineering team has implemented a mitigation (describe). You may have seen failed requests or latency. We will follow up with a detailed postmortem and any credit eligibility. For urgent support, reply to this email and our on-call will prioritize.

4) Postmortem and retro template

Title, Author, Date
Severity classification and duration
Timeline (UTC) — 5–15 minute resolution bullets. Example:
- 14:02 Alert triggered: 5xx rate > 20% on *service-api*
- 14:04 IC declared Sev-1; bridge open
- 14:10 Canary rollback initiated

Root cause statement (concise)
Impact statement (who, what, how long, customer list)
Contributing factors (short bullets)
Remediations (short-term and long-term) with owners and due dates
Follow-ups (PRs, tests, runbook updates)
Action verification plan (how we will validate fixes)

Postmortem review cadence: postmortem must be presented at next SRE retrospective (weekly) and given a severity tag in the incident index.

5) Practice lab (game-day) curriculum and rubric

Goals: validate orchestration patterns, exercise IC role, validate status-page cadence and customer messaging, and practice runbook updates.

Suggested quarterly schedule:
- Warm-up (30m): walk-through of alert sources and runbook template.
- Simulation (90m): live drill with synthetic alert that triggers a Sev-2 -> escalates to Sev-1 via injection script.- Post-exercise debrief (30m): immediate 15-minute hot retro followed by a written retrospective within 48 hours.

Exercise design templates:
- Scenario A: Upstream datastore latency spike causing KV cache thrash. Failure mode: gradual error increase over 10 minutes. Goal: test fast containment pattern (cache bypass + autoscaling).
- Scenario B: Canary release introduces tokenization regression that increases per-request latency. Failure mode: sharp regression after deploy. Goal: test canary rollback and customer comms.

Evaluation rubric (pass/fail criteria):
- IC assigned within SLA? (5m target)
- Bridge opened and roles assigned?
- Status page initial notice within 10m?
- Containment action taken within 15m?
- Post-exercise runbook update created?

6) Maintenance and governance

Runbook lifecycle:
- Each runbook must have an owner and a monthly checksum review.
- After a real incident, the runbook author must update the runbook within 7 days.
- Retire and archive runbooks older than 18 months unless validated in a game-day.

Metrics to track:
- Mean time to detect (MTTD)
- Mean time to containment (MTTC)
- Mean time to recovery (MTTR)
- Game-day pass rate (quarterly)

7) Appendix: quick commands and monitoring queries

Prometheus example (error rate over 5 minutes):
```
sum(rate(http_requests_total{job=\"service-api\",status=~\"5..\"}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{job=\"service-api\"}[5m]))
```

Kubernetes: fetch recent deploys and rollout status:
```
kubectl rollout history deploy/service-api -n prod --revision=3
kubectl get pods -n prod -l app=service-api -o wide
```
